Some things will last for a long time with little or no negative impact. "planned obsolescence" sounds like a dirty ploy to get more money, but it can be necessary. You need to design devices with a length of service in mind. It can be a few years or a few hundred. This greatly affects how the product turns out. For newspaper or flowers, a transitory resource, it may make little difference. However, if a car is designed for a few months, it's a race car. You get the most out of it and have a lot of money to keep it at peak performance. If it's for a few years in the public sector, then it's considered a bad design (and rightly so), but if a car is designed to last 100 years, it will be inefficient, under powered, heavy, expensive, and nobody would purchase it. Designers and engineers typically try to strike a balance that the majority of people seem to want, and it is pretty realistic to take a 30 year design and keep it running for quite some time after that if you are willing to put in the resources.
